title: 'Like a wailing woman'
short: Gilgamish weeps for Enkidu like a professional mourning woman.
body: Mourning was a role of women, sometimes professionals. The hero who once refused Ishtar now takes on a woman's role in grief. The comparison is one of several that cast the friendship in domestic and marital terms (he veils the corpse 'like a bride'). The opening of Tablet VIII in George's text is a long lament addressed to the mountains, rivers, animals and people who knew Enkidu, all called upon to weep for him. Thompson's version preserves only part of the address to the elders.

title: 'Wild ass, panther of the wild'
short: Thompson makes Enkidu one who chased the wild ass and the leopard; George reads these as epithets of Enkidu himself.
body: In George's text Gilgamish addresses his friend with animal epithets: wild ass, donkey of the uplands, panther. The animal epithets recall Enkidu's origins among the beasts. The difference shows how ambiguous Akkadian syntax can be. The line is repeated in Tablet X. Thompson's note offers the alternative 'dog' for one of the animals. Either way, the lament recalls the friends' shared life in the wild.

title: Death as sleep
short: Gilgamish asks what sleep has seized his friend: death and sleep are linked throughout the poem.
body: Gilgamish later fails the test of sleep (XI), and Uta-Napishtim says the dead and the sleeping are alike (X). The heart that no longer beats is detected by touch: a realistic and moving detail. The question is both naive and profound: Gilgamish at first cannot believe in death, and touches the heart to find it still. The motif of death as an unwaking sleep runs from this lament through Uta-Napishtim's speech in Tablet X to the sleep test in Tablet XI.

title: 'He veiled his friend like a bride'
short: Gilgamish covers Enkidu's face like a bride: the image fuses funeral and wedding.
body: Veiling the bride was part of the Mesopotamian wedding ceremony. The simile connects with the dreams of Tablet I, where Gilgamish embraces the meteor and axe 'like a wife'. Interpreters disagree whether such imagery implies a sexual relationship or uses marriage as the strongest available metaphor for love. George reads the line in the same way, and the image is widely discussed in studies of the friendship.

title: 'Like a lioness robbed of her whelps'
short: Gilgamish circles his friend like a lioness deprived of her cubs: a simile famously paralleled in the Iliad.
body: Akhilleus, mourning Patroclus, groans like a lion whose cubs have been stolen by a hunter (Iliad 18.318-322). The parallel is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for comparisons between the two epics, though direct influence cannot be proved. Both mourning heroes then plan elaborate funerals for their friends. The Gilgamesh simile uses a lioness, the Homeric one a bearded lion, but the emotional logic is the same: grief expressed as the rage and restless pacing of a bereaved animal.

anchor: on a couch of great size
title: Enkidu's funeral
short: Gilgamish repeats Shamash's words: he will lay Enkidu on a great couch and make Uruk mourn for him.
body: The fulfilment of Shamash's promise from Tablet VII. In George's fuller text the funeral includes a statue of Enkidu and a display of grave goods offered to the gods of the underworld, each named with a gift. Mourning gestures (tearing hair, wearing skins) mark Gilgamish's transformation. The repetition of Shamash's words shows Gilgamish fulfilling the god's promise point by point.

title: The Anunnaki
short: The Anunnaki are a group of great gods, here of the underworld.
body: Thompson's note: 'Spirits of the earth over whom Enlil was lord.' In earlier texts the Anunnaki are the great gods in general; in later texts they are often the gods of the underworld, as opposed to the Igigi of heaven. They appear again with torches in the Flood (XI). Here the 'Judge of the Anunnaki' is probably a god of the underworld who receives Enkidu.

title: Gilgamish's 'concept'
short: Thompson's 'concept' is a tentative rendering of an obscure line; modern editions read a commission for a statue of Enkidu.
body: The line is obscure. Thompson's rendering is tentative and the tablet is broken here. Modern editions read a call to craftsmen to make a statue of the dead friend in precious materials. The tablet is broken, but the making of a statue of a dead person was a known Mesopotamian practice, and a statue would provide a physical focus for the funerary cult. George's commentary discusses the craftsmen and materials listed for the image of Enkidu.

title: Funerary offerings
short: Honey in a carnelian bowl and cream in a lapis bowl are offered to Shamash: funerary gifts.
body: Thompson's notes identify the 'ruby' as sandu-stone. George's text shows Gilgamish presenting gifts to each underworld deity to welcome Enkidu. Honey, cream and precious vessels were typical gifts. In the fuller text the gifts are laid out in the sun, with Shamash as witness, and each is dedicated to an underworld deity (Ereshkigal, Dumuzi and others) so that they will welcome Enkidu and walk at his side. The care for the dead friend's reception below contrasts with the bleak picture of the underworld in Enkidu's dream (VII).
